reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Recurrent episodes of involuntary eating or drinking during partial arousals from sleep, with reduced or absent awareness and poor recall the next morning
Patients may consume high-calorie, peculiar or even inedible or toxic substances during episodes
Injuries can occur from handling kitchen equipment or eating while not fully awake
It is considered a non-REM parasomnia and frequently coexists with sleepwalking, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements
Sedative-hypnotics, particularly zolpidem, are well-recognised precipitants
It differs from night eating syndrome, in which the person is fully awake and consciously eats during nocturnal awakenings
Management targets any underlying parasomnia or restless legs, withdrawal of precipitating drugs, and a safe sleep and kitchen environment
reference.pathophysiology: Sleep-related eating disorder is regarded as a disorder of arousal, a non-REM parasomnia in which incomplete transition from deep sleep to wakefulness allows automatic feeding behaviour to occur while consciousness and memory systems remain largely offline. Conditions that fragment sleep, such as restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, and drugs that promote complex sleep-related behaviours, especially certain hypnotics, lower the threshold for these partial arousals and the associated eating.
additionalDifferentials: Night eating syndrome with conscious nocturnal eating
Nocturnal binge eating of a primary eating disorder
additionalInvestigations: Collateral history and a food diary documenting nocturnal eating and the degree of awareness
Review of medications, especially sedative-hypnotics such as zolpidem
Screening for restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder
Video-polysomnography when the diagnosis is unclear or seizures are suspected
Assessment for a coexisting daytime eating disorder or mood disorder
redFlags: Ingestion of toxic or inedible substances
Injuries or fire risk from cooking during episodes
Features suggesting nocturnal seizures rather than a parasomnia
Significant weight gain or metabolic consequences
reference.prognosis: The disorder tends to be chronic if untreated, but many patients improve substantially once precipitating drugs are stopped and any underlying restless legs or arousal disorder is treated; safety measures reduce the risk of injury in the meantime.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the fully conscious night eating syndrome
Overlooking zolpidem or another hypnotic as the trigger
Missing coexisting restless legs syndrome that is driving the arousals
Neglecting kitchen and home safety, leaving a risk of injury or fire
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Withdraw or switch precipitating drugs, particularly sedative-hypnotics such as zolpidem
Diagnose and treat underlying sleep disorders, including restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements with dopaminergic agents, and any coexisting parasomnia
Institute sleep-environment safety measures, securing food, hazardous substances and kitchen appliances to prevent injury and harmful ingestion
Consider pharmacotherapy such as topiramate where episodes persist despite removal of precipitants
Optimise sleep hygiene and treat any comorbid mood or daytime eating disorder
Refer to sleep medicine and arrange video-polysomnography where the diagnosis is unclear or seizures are suspected
